211.title: At-Takwir: the sun wrapped
211.hook: when the sun is folded up and the stars fall (81:1–2)
211.howItsDone: Many Muslims read At-Takwir together with Al-Infitar and Al-Inshiqaq as a picture of the Day of Resurrection, following a hadith that recommends them for that purpose; its opening is among the most widely memorized passages of the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Infitar, the sky cleaves, and a body created, fashioned and balanced. Your line was shaped in proportion.

The most reliable thing you know isn't a person or a job. It's something that has never once let you down. For almost everyone, it's the sun. It came up this morning. It came up the day you were born, and the day your grandparents were born. Every plan anyone has ever made assumes it. Now a voice begins: when the sun is folded up. The surah just before Al-Infitar starts right there, with the one thing nobody doubts, and keeps going, a long list of whens. Today: At-Takwir, the sun wrapped.
screen: `THE MOST RELIABLE THING YOU KNOW.` → `WHEN THE SUN IS FOLDED UP.` → `AT-TAKWIR, THE SUN WRAPPED.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-one begins, in Pickthall's words: When the sun is overthrown, And when the stars fall. The Arabic verb is kuwwirat, from takwir, a picture from everyday clothing. Kawwara is what you do with a turban: wind the cloth around and around until it's wrapped up. So the sun, which spreads its light across everything, is wound up like cloth and put away. Then the list rolls on. The stars fall and dim. The mountains are moved. The camels ten months pregnant, the most precious thing a family in Arabia could own, are left untended, because nobody is thinking about wealth anymore. The wild animals are gathered. The seas are set alight. Twelve whens in all, and after them, one line: then a soul will know what it has brought. A hadith in Tirmidhi says that whoever wants to see the Day of Resurrection as if with their own eyes should read this surah, and Al-Infitar, and Al-Inshiqaq, the three just walked through. Another hadith in Tirmidhi reports that when Abu Bakr told the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ his hair had turned gray, he named a few surahs that had done it, and this was one. So why start with the sun? Because if even the sun can be wrapped and put away, so can everything. Every tower, every fortune, every plan. The Qur'an says it elsewhere plainly: everyone upon the earth will pass away, and the face of your Lord remains. That isn't meant to make life feel pointless. It tells you where the one thing that lasts is.
screen: `KUWWIRAT — WOUND UP LIKE A TURBAN.` · `THE PRECIOUS CAMELS, LEFT UNTENDED.` · `TWELVE WHENS, THEN ONE SOUL.` · `IF EVEN THE SUN, THEN EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING ENDS BUT HIM.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you that feels permanent, a wall, a table, a heavy old book: it was made, and one day it won't be here. Then bring to mind something heavier, a worry you've carried for months or a win you're proud of, and hold it lightly, the way you'd hold cloth you're about to fold and put away. Notice what's still here: your breath, this moment, and the One Muslims say remains.
At-Takwir. The wrapping up, the sun wound like a turban, and the name of Surah eighty-one. Today's word.
Your line: everything ends but him. If the sun can be wrapped, a worry or a win can sit a little lighter. Until tomorrow.

212.title: At-Takwir: the buried girl
212.hook: when the baby girl buried alive is asked for what sin she was killed (81:8–9)
212.howItsDone: Muslims read these verses as the Qur'an's condemnation of female infanticide; the hadith on raising daughters is quoted at the birth of a girl, and the 'aqiqah, a sacrifice and a shared meal of thanks, is held for daughters as well as sons.

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Takwir, the sun wound up like a turban and put away. Your line was everything ends but him.

Among the twelve whens of At-Takwir, the sun wrapped, the stars falling, the seas on fire, one isn't about the sky at all. It's about a single child. Of everything the surah could show on the last day, the biggest events in the universe, it stops for one small girl whom nobody in her own world stopped for. Today's lesson is a hard one, and it's told gently. It's about who gets to speak on that day, and who has to answer.
screen: `THE SUN, THE STARS, THE SEAS.` → `AND ONE SMALL GIRL.` → `THE BURIED GIRL.`

segments.voice: Verses eight and nine, in Pickthall's words: "And when the girl-child that was buried alive is asked For what sin she was slain." Commentators say that in pre-Islamic Arabia some people killed newborn daughters. The Qur'an itself names two reasons: fear of poverty, and fear of shame. Elsewhere it describes the reaction: when one of them is told a daughter has been born, his face darkens, and he hides from people, wondering whether to keep her in humiliation or bury her in the dust. The Qur'an forbade it outright: do not kill your children for fear of poverty. Now look at how verse nine is built. The question isn't put to the father. It's put to her. For what sin was she killed? Commentators notice this. The one who had no voice in her short life is the one addressed on that day, in front of everyone, and her answer will be the testimony. The question holds its own answer: no sin. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ went further than forbidding. A hadith in Muslim's collection says that whoever raises two daughters until they grow up will come on the Day of Resurrection with him, and he held his fingers together to show how close. He had daughters himself, and was known for standing up to greet Fatima when she came into the room. So the surah names the harm and gives the girl the question, and the Prophet's practice turns the shame upside down: raising a daughter becomes a way to be close to him.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a girl or woman in your life, a daughter, a sister, a niece, a mother, a student, a friend, and picture her face. Think of one thing about her that deserves to be honored out loud: her courage, her humor, her work. If there's no one close, hold in mind girls anywhere whose lives aren't valued.
At-Takwir. The wrapping up, Surah eighty-one, where the buried girl is asked for what sin she was killed. Today's word.
Your line: she will be asked. The one silenced in life is the one given the question. Day two hundred twelve.

213.title: 'Abasa: he frowned
213.hook: the Prophet ﷺ turned from a blind man to talk to the powerful, and was corrected (80:1–10)
213.carry: turn to the one who came
213.howItsDone: Muslims cite 'Abasa as a lesson that sincerity outweighs status; Ibn Umm Maktum is remembered as a companion and muezzin, and the surah sits in Juz' 'Amma, the thirtieth part of the Qur'an, often learned by heart early.

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Takwir, and the buried girl who is given the question. Your line was she will be asked.

A work event. You're finally talking to the one person in the room who could change everything: the investor, the boss's boss, the person with the answer. Then a tap on your shoulder. The intern, or an old neighbor, asking a question that could wait. You don't say anything rude. Your face just does a small thing. A flicker. A frown. It would be easy never to think about it again. The surah just before At-Takwir is named after that flicker. And the surprise is whose face it was. Today: 'Abasa, he frowned.
screen: `FINALLY TALKING TO THE RIGHT PERSON.` → `A TAP ON THE SHOULDER.` → `'ABASA, HE FROWNED.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty opens, in Pickthall's words: He frowned and turned away Because the blind man came unto him. Sunni commentators, following reports in Tirmidhi and the tafsir, explain the scene this way. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was in Mecca, speaking with leaders of the Quraysh, hoping they would listen. A blind man, 'Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, came up asking to be taught. The Prophet frowned and turned back to the leaders, and revelation came correcting him. Shia commentators such as al-Tabataba'i, and some others, read it differently: the one who frowned was another man present, not the Prophet. Both readings are held with care. Now listen to how the correction is spoken. It begins in the third person, he frowned, which commentators read as courtesy, the text almost looking away. Then it speaks directly: what could tell you, perhaps he would grow in purity, or be reminded, and the reminder would help him. As for the one who thinks he needs nothing, you give him your attention. But the one who came to you eagerly, and in awe, him you neglect. And the correction stays in the text, recited ever since. What happened next? Ibn Umm Maktum became a caller to prayer in Medina, alongside Bilal, and reports say the Prophet left him in charge of the prayer in Medina when he traveled. The man turned away from became the voice calling the city to prayer.

segments.voice: Think of the people who come to you and are easy to overlook: the quiet coworker, the kid who wants to show you something, the older relative who repeats a story, the person at the counter. Pick one, and picture the next time they come to you, and you turn fully toward them: phone down, eyes up, full attention.
'Abasa. He frowned, the name of Surah eighty, which turns our attention to the one who came eagerly. Today's word.

214.title: 'Abasa: look at your food
214.hook: let the human look at his food: rain, grain, grapes, olives, palms (80:24–32)
214.tomorrow: 'Abasa: the day a man flees his brother
214.howItsDone: Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after, eat with the right hand, and try not to waste food; these verses of 'Abasa are recalled as a reminder that a meal begins with rain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'Abasa, he frowned, and the blind man who came eagerly. Your line was turn to the one who came.
screen: `'ABASA — TURN TO THE ONE WHO CAME.`

segments.voice: Where did your last meal come from? The quick answer is usually a store, a delivery bag, a drive-through window. Maybe a plastic tray with a sticker on it. The food shows up already finished, with the whole story cut off. Somewhere there was rain, and dirt, and a seed, and months of sun, and people bent over in a field. None of that is on the sticker. 'Abasa, after the story of the frown, turns to a very different subject, and asks for a slower kind of looking.
screen: `A TRAY WITH A STICKER.` → `THE STORY CUT OFF.` → `LOOK AT YOUR FOOD.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-four, in Pickthall's words: Let man consider his food. Look at it. Then the surah tells the story behind the plate, starting in the sky. We pour water down in showers. Then We split the earth open, in clefts. Then We cause grain to grow in it, and grapes, and green fodder, and olive trees and date palms, and gardens thick with trees, and fruit, and grasses. Provision for you, and for your animals. Rain, cracked soil, a sprout, a harvest, like a slow-motion film of a seed. The whole cycle is a gift, set down in front of you. One word in that list is famous for a different reason: abb, grasses. A report in the commentaries says that 'Umar, one of the closest companions, read this verse, admitted he didn't know exactly what abb meant, and decided not to force a meaning onto it. Commentators explain it as pasture, the plants that animals graze. But the honesty is worth keeping: even 'Umar could say, I don't know exactly. Notice where the passage sits: right after the surah reminds the human being he was made from a drop, and asks why he is ungrateful. The answer to ingratitude isn't a lecture. It's: look at your plate. Trace one bite back to the rain. Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after: two small words to bracket the story.

215.title: 'Abasa: the day a man flees his brother
215.hook: on that day each flees mother, father, wife and children (80:34–37)
215.howItsDone: Muslims read the end of 'Abasa as a description of the Day of Resurrection, and some take it as a reason to keep family ties, silat al-rahim, strong now, visiting parents and relatives and mending quarrels.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'Abasa, and a meal traced back to the rain. Your line was look at your food.

A crowded family photo. Grandparents in the middle, cousins squeezed in at the edges, someone's kid making a face. When the worst happens, these are the people a family runs toward, not away. The end of 'Abasa describes a day when that instinct runs the other way. It's an unsettling image, and commentators don't read it as fear for its own sake. It says something about today, while the photo is still full.
screen: `A CROWDED FAMILY PHOTO.` → `WHEN THE WORST HAPPENS, FAMILY RUNS TOWARD.` → `A DAY IT RUNS THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Verse thirty-three: when the deafening blast comes. The word is as-sakhkhah, which commentators explain as a sound so loud it strikes the ears. Then verse thirty-four, in Pickthall's words: On the day when a man fleeth from his brother. The list goes on: and his mother and his father, and his wife and his children. Commentators notice the order. It moves inward: a brother, the parents who raised you, the spouse beside you, your own children, the closest of all. The closest circle of a life, one ring at a time, and each one fled. Why? Verse thirty-seven: every one of them, that day, will have concern enough of his own. Not cruelty. Overwhelm. Each person alone with their own record, as At-Takwir put it: a soul will know what it has brought. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim adds a human moment. Aisha heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ describe people raised on that day, and asked: wouldn't they look at one another? He answered that the matter would be too serious for that. In one version, in Tirmidhi, he recited verse thirty-seven. Then the surah ends with faces, as Al-Ghashiyah did. Some bright, laughing, rejoicing. Some covered in dust. So what is it for? Some readers hear it not as a reason to fear family, but the opposite. That day, each is alone. Today, no one has to be. The brother can still be called, the mother visited, the child held. Read that way, the verse makes the present precious, because it won't always be like this.
screen: `AS-SAKHKHAH — THE DEAFENING BLAST.` · `BROTHER, PARENTS, SPOUSE, CHILDREN.` · `CONCERN ENOUGH OF HIS OWN.` · `THAT DAY ALONE. TODAY, NOT.` · then, large: `EACH ALONE THAT DAY.`

segments.voice: Picture the people closest to you, one ring at a time: a sibling or a friend like one, your parents or whoever raised you, a partner, children if you have them, or the young people you love. Let each face come clearly; today they are all within reach. Rest on the one you'd most like to hold close today, a call, a visit, a long hug.

216.howItsDone: Muslims believe angels take each soul at death; many pray for an easy passing, and at a deathbed family often recite the shahada gently and read Qur'an, hoping the soul is drawn out with ease.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of 'Abasa, a day when each person flees even their own family. Your line was each alone that day.

If you've ever sat with someone at the end of their life, you may remember the breathing most. Long pauses. The room holding still. Then a breath goes out and doesn't come back in. People who've been there often say it was quieter than they expected, and sometimes, strangely, peaceful. Every tradition has had to find words for that moment. The surah just before 'Abasa opens with its own, in a pair of oaths that are hard to translate and have been read several ways.
screen: `THE LAST BREATH IN A QUIET ROOM.` → `QUIETER THAN EXPECTED.` → `AN-NAZI'AT, THOSE WHO PULL OUT.`

segments.voice: Surah seventy-nine begins with an oath: by those who pull out, forcefully. Then: by those who draw out, gently. The first word, an-nazi'at, comes from a root meaning to pull, to wrench something out. The second, an-nashitat, has a softer picture behind it: loosening a knot, or easing a bucket up out of a well. The surah doesn't say who these are. Most commentators say angels, the ones who take souls at death: from some the soul is pulled out hard, from others drawn out gently. Other early commentators read stars moving across the sky, or death itself, or arrows drawn from a bow. The text leaves it open, and so have the scholars. But the angels reading is the one most Muslims know, and a long hadith, reported in Abu Dawud and in Ahmad's collection, fills it in. When a believer dies, it says, the soul leaves as easily as a drop of water flows from the mouth of a waterskin. For others, it is dragged like a skewer through wet wool. Hard to hear. But the surah doesn't stop at the hard picture. The very next oath is gently. Many Muslims pray for exactly this, an easy departure, and ask at the bedsides of the dying for the soul to be drawn out gently. In this reading, death isn't a stranger crashing in. It's a door that's attended. Someone is sent; someone does the drawing out. As Muslims read these verses, nobody leaves unaccompanied.
screen: `AN-NAZI'AT — PULLED OUT HARD.` · `AN-NASHITAT — A KNOT LOOSENED.` · `ANGELS, STARS, OR DEATH ITSELF.` · `NOBODY LEAVES UNACCOMPANIED.` · then, large: `GENTLY DRAWN.`

segments.voice: Watch your breath going out, not in. Let each exhale be slow and complete, like water poured from a jug until it's empty, and notice the small pause at the bottom before the next breath comes on its own. Nothing to fix: just the out-breath, gently drawn, and the one that comes after.
An-Nazi'at. Those who pull out, the opening word of Surah seventy-nine, paired with those who draw out gently. Today's word.
Your line: gently drawn. Even the hard picture has a gentle one beside it. That's day two hundred sixteen.

217.title: An-Nazi'at: Musa, again
217.hook: go to Pharaoh, he has transgressed, and ask, would you purify yourself (79:17–19)
217.howItsDone: Muslims read Musa's mission to Pharaoh as a model of calling others with gentle speech, following the instruction in Ta-Ha to speak to him gently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: An-Nazi'at, and souls drawn out, some hard, some gently. Your line was gently drawn.

The boss who humiliates people in meetings. The relative who only hears himself. Being sent to someone like that with a message he won't want usually means rehearsing a speech or a fight. The Qur'an tells the story of Musa, Moses, in more than one surah, and early on this path you followed him as far as the fire in the valley of Tuwa. In An-Nazi'at he comes back, briefly, sent to a hard listener indeed: Pharaoh, a king who calls himself a god. And the first thing Musa is told to say isn't a threat. It's a question.
screen: `A HARD PERSON TO TALK TO.` → `A KING WHO CALLS HIMSELF A GOD.` → `MUSA, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Verse fifteen asks: has the story of Musa reached you? His Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa: go to Pharaoh; he has transgressed. And say to him, verse eighteen: would you like to purify yourself? And I will guide you to your Lord, so you'll hold Him in awe. An invitation, in the form of a question, to a ruler who will soon call himself lord. The verb is tazakka, from the root z-k-y. You've met that root twice on this stretch: in Ash-Shams, successful is the one who purifies the soul, and in Al-A'la, successful is the one who purifies himself. Now a word from the same root is offered to Pharaoh. Even he is invited to the thing that makes a soul succeed. In Surah Ta-Ha, Musa and his brother Harun are told the same in other words: speak to him gently, perhaps he will remember or fear. Then Musa shows him the great sign. Pharaoh denies, turns away, gathers his people, and proclaims: I am your lord, the most high. Al-a'la, the very word from the surah two weeks back. A man claiming the title of the Most High. And he is seized. The surah ends the story: in this is a lesson for whoever holds God in awe. It's the end of a week, too: the sun wrapped and the buried girl given her question; the frown, the food, the day each person flees; souls gently drawn; and now a question offered to a tyrant. Nobody, the surah suggests, is beyond being asked.
screen: `THE SACRED VALLEY OF TUWA.` · `A QUESTION, NOT A THREAT.` · `TAZAKKA — OFFERED EVEN TO PHARAOH.` · `I AM YOUR LORD THE MOST HIGH.` · then, large: `WOULD YOU PURIFY YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you find hard to talk to: not the worst person in the world, just someone where every conversation goes badly. Picture opening the next one with a real question instead of a point, like: what would help? How are you, really? Choose the words.
